extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors writing query letters to literary agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing query letters and pitches to literary agents, highlighting common mistakes that trigger immediate rejection and the positive qualities of an effective one-page query.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries that have typos in the first sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Having spelling or grammatical mistakes — especially in the very first sentence of a query letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typos in the opening signal carelessness and can lead to immediate rejection; proofread carefully before sending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries that start with a nugget of wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening with a trite aphorism or generic piece of wisdom (example given: “Every step we take in life moves us in a direction.”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such openings are cliché and do not serve the purpose of a query; they waste space and fail to engage an agent with the book's premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries with very small type, florid or unconventional fonts, and whacky background colors
rubrics_metrics.description: Using tiny font sizes, overly decorative/unusual typefaces, or colored backgrounds in the query letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These choices strain readers' eyes and appear unprofessional. Use readable, conventional formatting—agents likely suffer from eyestrain and prefer clean presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries longer than one page
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting a query letter that exceeds one page in length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long queries suggest the manuscript may be overwritten; keep queries to one page maximum to respect agents' time and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries with overcomplicated directions for replying
rubrics_metrics.description: Including convoluted or unnecessary instructions about how/when to contact you (example: lengthy travel/availability details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep contact information simple—provide a straightforward street or email address. Overly detailed availability instructions are unnecessary and off-putting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries with all the agents in New York in the “To” line
rubrics_metrics.description: Addressing a single submission to multiple agents at once (i.e., listing many agents in the To line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This appears unprofessional and disrespectful of agents' individuality; target queries appropriately rather than mass-addressing agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries that start by telling the agent you won't take up their time
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening with phrases like “I know how busy you are, so I’ll get straight to the point and not take up too much of your valuable time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements are self-defeating (they already waste space) and come off as performative; instead open with a concise, compelling hook about the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries that make grandiose claims about sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Making unrealistic or sweeping sales claims (example: predicting the book will sell 150 million copies because it appeals to all women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents view grandiose market claims skeptically; focus on realistic, specific positioning or comparable titles rather than hyperbolic projections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries that emphasize hard work instead of quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements like “I’ve worked very hard on this novel,” implying effort equals publishability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effort alone doesn't prove quality. Demonstrate the book's merits through the pitch (hook, premise, stakes, voice) rather than asserting how hard you worked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Queries that declare the obvious (e.g., "I have written a fiction novel")
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating self-evident facts about the manuscript (example: “I have written a fiction novel.”) that signal a lack of understanding about genre or conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stating the obvious; doing so suggests the writer may not understand basic publishing conventions and may not be ready to be published. Use precise, informative descriptors instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doesn't state the obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: A good query avoids stating obvious facts about the work; if it states the obvious, agents may think the book is all telling and no showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on vivid, specific details that demonstrate voice and premise rather than flat summaries of self-evident information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is never longer than one page
rubrics_metrics.description: A good query letter should never exceed one page; overlong queries make agents suspect the manuscript is overwritten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the pitch concise—tighten prose to fit one page, prioritizing the hook, brief synopsis, and relevant credentials or comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is not about you
rubrics_metrics.description: A good query focuses on the book rather than the author's personal life; if it's about the author, agents may assume it's navel-gazing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit author biography to relevant publication credits or qualifications; let the book's premise, voice, and market positioning be foregrounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never sounds generic
rubrics_metrics.description: A good query must avoid generic language; generic queries lead agents to think the book lacks a unique or appealing voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific, distinctive language and show a sense of voice in the pitch so the agent can sense what sets the book apart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Makes the book sound interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: A good query makes the book sound interesting; if it doesn't, agents will conclude the book isn't interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a compelling hook and concise synopsis that convey stakes, conflict, and voice to entice the agent to request more.
